Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Why does AI need so much electricity and water? A chatbot is not just software in the cloud: it runs on huge, hot buildings full of computers. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Nova Scotians rally against an AI data centre that Anthropic plans to use. On Saturday people held at least seven rallies across Nova Scotia, Canada, against a planned C$10 billion AI data centre at Point Tupper; the Halifax rally alone drew close to 2,000 people by one local estimate. Anthropic, the company that makes Claude (which writes this email), has agreed to rent computing capacity there. Protesters want a pause and proper rules; the provincial government and the developer say it will not harm the environment or raise electricity bills. Read more and the background.
  • Claude helps scientists picture a mysterious cell structure found in bacteria. Anthropic’s biology team says that, working with Claude, it found relatives of a mysterious cell capsule called a “vault” in bacteria and took the first detailed 3D picture of one; human scientists did the lab work and Claude searched billions of proteins and processed the images. Anthropic makes Claude, which writes this email. It is a preprint not yet checked by outside scientists, Anthropic lists Claude’s own mistakes, and what vaults are for remains a mystery. Read more and the background.
  • France’s top literary prize goes to a novel with one ChatGPT sentence in it. The winner of France’s top literary prize, the Goncourt, says he used ChatGPT three times while writing his novel, including one sentence he put in deliberately “to play with the reader”, and told the jury only after he won. He says writers cannot pretend AI does not exist but must keep it in its place; readers are divided. This comes from a Euronews report on his radio interview. Read more and the background.
  • AI money in the US elections: lots spent, mixed results. In the US elections, groups funded by people in the AI industry spent millions, with mixed results: several candidates backed by the biggest pro-industry network lost, and a group backed by Anthropic (which makes Claude, the AI writing this email) did better with Democrats than Republicans. The fight is over whether Washington should set one national rulebook for AI that overrides the states. It is hard to say how much the money mattered, since Democrats did well everywhere. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Scientists sketch an AI that could understand whole ecosystems, Roche signs up an AI start-up to help design new medicines.

Answer to the question of the day. Every answer a chatbot gives is worked out on powerful chips in a data centre, a large building packed with computers. Teaching a big model in the first place means running thousands of those chips flat out for weeks, and after that every single question uses electricity again; researchers estimate a chatbot question uses several times more power than an ordinary web search. All that work turns into heat, and many data centres cool their machines with water, some of which evaporates. Because companies are building new data centres faster than new clean power stations, much of the electricity still comes from fossil fuels. How big the problem is depends on where a data centre is and how it is powered and cooled, and exact figures are disputed. The article below, from MIT, explains the causes clearly. Adam Zewe, “Explained: Generative AI’s environmental impact” (MIT News, January 2025).
